nameStory: The elktoe gets its name from the distinctive tooth-like ridges inside its shell that resembled an elk's hoof to early naturalists. These internal "teeth" help lock the two halves of the shell together, much like how an elk's cloven hoof has two distinct parts that work as one.
description: The elktoe is a freshwater mussel that spends its life buried partway in the sandy or muddy bottoms of rivers and streams. Like all mussels, it's a bivalve with two hinged shells that protect its soft body inside. These filter-feeders pump water through their bodies to catch tiny particles of food, and they can live for decades in the same spot. Adult elktoes typically reach 2-4 inches in length.

idTips.label: Shell Shape
idTips.description: Oval to slightly rectangular shell that feels smooth when you run your finger along it, with a subtle ridge running from the pointed front end toward the back

idTips.label: Shell Color
idTips.description: Dark brown to blackish exterior that may feel slightly rough or bumpy, sometimes with faint growth rings visible like tree rings

idTips.label: Interior Surface
idTips.description: Inside of shell is pearly white or bluish-white with a smooth, almost slippery feel when touched

idTips.label: Hinge Teeth
idTips.description: Two distinct ridged teeth near the front hinge that feel firm and sharp when gently pressed with a fingernail

idTips.label: Size Range
idTips.description: Adult shells typically span the width of an adult's palm, feeling surprisingly heavy for their size due to the thick shell

habitat: Elktoes live in clean, flowing rivers and larger streams with sandy or gravelly bottoms throughout New England. They prefer areas with moderate current where they can filter-feed effectively, often found partially buried in substrate near deeper pools or runs. Look for them in watersheds that haven't been heavily impacted by pollution or sedimentation.

seasonality.spring: Best time to spot elktoes as spring floods may expose shells along shorelines, and clearer water after snowmelt makes underwater viewing easier.
seasonality.summer: Mussels are most active in warm water, occasionally extending their siphons above the sediment surface. Low water levels may reveal more individuals.
seasonality.fall: Good viewing continues with clear water, though mussels begin to slow their activity as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: Mussels remain buried and largely inactive under ice, making this the most difficult season for observation.

funFact: Elktoe mussels are ecosystem engineers that can filter up to 10 gallons of water per day, and a healthy mussel bed can make river water noticeably clearer downstream - they're like living water treatment plants!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other dark-shelled river mussels, but the elktoe's distinctive hinge teeth and relatively smooth, oval shell help distinguish it. Memory trick: "Elk-toe has the teeth to show" - those internal ridges are the key feature.
contextualKnowledge: Despite their name suggesting a connection to elk, these mussels are found well outside elk range in New England. The name comes purely from the shell's internal structure, not from any ecological relationship with the large mammals.
compareHints: Unlike the Triangle Floater which has a more angular, triangular shell shape, the elktoe is more evenly oval. The Brook Floater tends to be thinner and more delicate-looking, while the elktoe feels more substantial and has a thicker shell. Both relatives also prefer slightly different water conditions, with elktoes favoring larger rivers over the smaller streams preferred by Brook Floaters.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Triangle Floaters are more angular than their Brook Floater cousins, which have rounder, more oval shells with smoother surfaces.
Brook floaters are smaller and prefer cleaner, smaller streams compared to their relatives the triangle floater and elktoe, which can tolerate larger rivers and slightly more disturbed conditions.
